passage: Teacher's note, Class 9 group assignment. During the poster work Bhavna spent most of the period "finding a marker" while the other three researched and wrote. Bhavna told me later, "They will finish it, they always do." Bhavna did not look proud, and looked away when I said the other three seemed worn out. The three said nothing, though one rolled her eyes and another sighed. I spoke with Bhavna privately and asked which part felt doable, and Bhavna picked the summary. I will check in on Friday. — Jahnavi Ma'am

qa.q: Which part did Bhavna pick after the private talk?
qa.a: Bhavna picked the summary.

qa.q: What does Bhavna's looking away when the others are called worn out suggest about how Bhavna feels?
qa.a: It suggests guilt and unease; Bhavna assumed the diligent ones would finish, and seems to sense it is not fair.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi Ma'am do that could change Bhavna's contribution?
qa.a: Jahnavi Ma'am spoke with Bhavna privately, asked which part felt doable and planned to check in on Friday, which gives a clear task and follow-up.

qa.q: What might the child who rolled her eyes be feeling?
qa.a: She may feel irritated and taken for granted, doing more than her share while saying nothing aloud.

grounding: A teenager does the minimum in a group project, assuming the diligent ones will finish, feeling a little guilty but rarely admitting it.

passage: Sunday. The group assignment on renewable energy is due Wednesday. Chetan messaged, "Harish, which section are you taking?" I sent a thumbs-up and did nothing. I wrote "will do tonight" three times. Priyal and Chetan are the serious ones. They will finish it; they always do. I feel a bit clever for sleeping in and a bit rotten, as if I am cheating without doing anything I could be blamed for. Nobody will know my slides are missing until the last minute. Last time Chetan just added them. I hate that I am counting on that. Maybe tomorrow I will actually do one slide. — Harish

qa.q: What did Harish send in reply to Chetan's message?
qa.a: Harish sent a thumbs-up and did nothing.

qa.q: Why does Harish feel both clever and rotten?
qa.a: Harish feels clever for getting away with doing nothing and rotten for relying on others; the guilt is private but real.

qa.q: What small step could Harish take today to break the pattern?
qa.a: Harish could tell Chetan which section will be done and by when, then finish one slide tonight, so the promise is visible.

qa.q: What might Chetan be feeling after adding Harish's slides last time?
qa.a: Chetan may feel tired and quietly resentful, having covered for Harish without saying so, and worried about being the one to fix it again.

grounding: A teenager does the minimum in a group project, assuming the diligent ones will finish, feeling a little guilty but clever, and rarely admits it.

passage:
You want to know a secret? I'm Gautam, and in Class 10 I was the smartest lazy person in our group.
For the geography project, Afreen made the charts, Sid did the model, and Pallavi wrote the report. I said I'd “handle the printing.” That was two pages at the shop.
I knew Afreen would never let the project fail. She stays up till two for everything. So I just waited.
We got an A. The teacher said, “Great teamwork.” I felt a little guilty, sure. But honestly, also kind of clever, like I'd found a shortcut.
I never told them. You're the first person I've said this to, and my face is getting hot saying it.

qa.q: What did Gautam say he would handle?
qa.a: Gautam said he'd handle the printing.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after the teacher said "Great teamwork"?
qa.a: Gautam felt a bit guilty but also clever, as if a shortcut had been found; now the memory brings embarrassment.

qa.q: What could Gautam do now to make it right?
qa.a: Gautam could thank Afreen honestly for carrying the project, and take a real share of the next group task.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel if she learned the truth?
qa.a: She might feel used and frustrated, having stayed up late while Gautam counted on her not letting it fail.

grounding: A teenager admits doing the minimum in a group project, assuming a diligent friend would finish it, and feeling guilty yet clever.

passage:
Week one: The history project group made a plan. Payal said she would do “some slides.” Then she went to badminton every evening. Harsh and Sneha will do it anyway, she thought. They always do.
Week two: Harsh messaged: “Payal, your slides?” She sent two, copied from her notes, at midnight. Harsh wrote back, “ok thanks,” and she could tell he redid them.
Week three: At the presentation, Payal spoke for one minute. The teacher praised “the whole team's effort.” Payal smiled. Inside she felt a pinch of guilt, and also a small secret pleasure, like getting away with something.
Later Sneha asked, “Was it fun doing your slides?” Payal laughed and changed the subject.

qa.q: How many slides did Payal send?
qa.a: She sent two.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when the teacher praised the whole team?
qa.a: She felt a pinch of guilt mixed with a small secret pleasure, as if she had got away with something.

qa.q: What went wrong in how the group split the work, and how could it be fixed?
qa.a: Payal's vague "some slides" let her coast; the group could have written who does which slides and by when.

qa.q: How might Harsh feel about redoing Payal's slides?
qa.a: He likely felt tired and resentful, but too polite to say more than "ok thanks".

grounding: Shows a teenager doing the minimum in a group project, assuming the diligent ones will finish, feeling guilty but clever and not admitting it.

passage:
Keerthana, since you're complaining about your lazy project partner, let me confess something. This is your Gopika chithi, and I was that lazy partner once.
Class 11, a biology project on pond water. Three of us. Asha and Revathi collected samples, looked through the microscope, wrote everything. I added the cover page and some drawings.
I was sure they'd finish. They always finished. And they did.
When we got full marks, I felt a little guilty, yes. But also smart, you know? Like I'd found the trick.
Years later, at a wedding, Revathi laughed and said, “You and your cover page!” She knew. She had always known. I wanted to sink into the floor.

qa.q: What did young Gopika add to the project?
qa.a: She added the cover page and some drawings.

qa.q: How did young Gopika feel when they got full marks?
qa.a: She felt a little guilty but also smart, as if she'd found a trick.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed Gopika the truth?
qa.a: Revathi's remark at the wedding showed that her friends had known all along, which left her deeply embarrassed.

qa.q: How might Revathi have felt back in Class 11?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and tired of carrying the work, but kept quiet at the time.

grounding: An elder admits having done the minimum in a school project, assuming diligent friends would finish, feeling guilty yet clever.

passage:
The history project was due at 8 a.m., and at 9 p.m. the power went out across the colony.
In the group chat, Jagdish was typing by torchlight: "Doing the timeline on paper, will send a photo." Rhea: "Finishing sources on my phone." Tara had gone quiet.
Chandrika lay on her bed under the dead fan and sent a thumbs-up. Her one job had been the title page, done in ten minutes last week. She'd known from the start that Jagdish would never let the project fail. That was the clever part, she told herself.
When Rhea wrote, "Anyone free to check dates?", Chandrika's thumb hovered. Then she put the phone face down.
At 7:50 the next morning Jagdish handed in the folder, eyes red. Ma'am said, "Great work, all four of you." Chandrika smiled along, and felt something small and sour in her stomach. She didn't mention the title page.

qa.q: What time did the power go out?
qa.a: At 9 p.m., across the colony.

qa.q: What did Chandrika feel when Ma'am praised all four of them?
qa.a: Chandrika felt a mix of relief and guilt, "something small and sour" in her stomach, knowing she had only done the title page.

qa.q: What could Chandrika have done when Rhea asked for help?
qa.a: She could have offered to check the dates, a small job she could do by phone even without power.

qa.q: What was the night like for Jagdish?
qa.a: Jagdish was likely worn out and a little resentful, working by torchlight until the red-eyed morning while sharing credit equally.

grounding: Shows a teenager doing the minimum on a group project, relying on the diligent ones, feeling half clever and half guilty and not admitting it.
